To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the LC-NE circuit mediates stress-induced anxiety and that CRH(+) inputs from the amygadala are critical for this effect.
increased tonic activity in the LC-NE neurons, but not phastic activity in these neurons, mediates anxiety-like and aversion behaviors induced by stress.

1) increased tonic activity of the LC-NE neurons mediates stress-induced anxiety, 2) increased tonic activity in the LC-NE can be induced by CRH inputs, and 3) CRH inputs to the LC are sufficient to induce anxiety-like behavior.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how the brain responds to stress and the consequences of that stress response.
understanding the neural circuits and mechanisms that mediate stress-induced anxiety and fear.
understanding the neurobiology of stress-related psychiatric disorders such as depression, anxiety and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) with the ultimate aim of developing new treatments.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
CRH engagement of the LC-NE circuit is necessary and sufficient to generate stress-related anxiety.
the LC-NE is a critical mediator of stress-induced anxiety and aversive behavior.
stress-induced activation of the LC-NE neurons induces anxiety-like behaviors and that this activation is mediated by CRH+ inputs from the amydgala.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the noradrenergics system in the locus coeruleus, a small brain structure, is critical in the generation of anxiety-like behaviors.
CRH+ neurons from the amygdalar central nucleus project to the locus coeruleus and increase the activity of the LC-NE neurons, resulting in anxiety-like behaviors.
the locus coeruleus is a critical mediator of stress-induced anxiety.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the LC-NE neurons play a critical role in mediating anxiety and aversion in response to stress.
stress-induced anxiety and aversive behavior can be mediated by the tonic activation of the locus coeruleus (LC), the major source of norepinephrine in the brain.
the LC-NE is the main driver of stress-induced anxiety.
